articles.title: Documents Reveal the Postal Service's Broad Surveillance of Political Activists
articles.content:
We know that mission creep is a thing, but is it entirely necessary for every federal agency to try to reimagine itself as Big Brother?
OK, silly question. Of course, it's not necessary for the Post Office—that's the agency under scrutiny this time—to engage in mass surveillance. It just seems to be an activity in which all government bureaucracies inevitably engage. That's the most logical explanation for why the U.S. Postal Service decided that it should monitor the internet for information about political demonstrations.
"The law enforcement arm of the U.S. Postal Service has been quietly running a program that tracks and collects Americans' social media posts, including those about planned protests," Jana Winter first reported in 2021 for Yahoo! News.
"Analysts with the United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) Internet Covert Operations Program (iCOP) monitored significant activity regarding planned protests occurring internationally and domestically on March 20, 2021," according to a March 2021 bulletin from the iCOP that was included in the article. "Locations and times have been identified for these protests, which are being distributed online across multiple social media platforms, to include right-wing leaning Parler and Telegram accounts."
Among the organizations alarmed by the disclosure was the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), which filed suit to learn more about the surveillance program. "After years of delays and technical failures that led the agency to lose access to a trove of emails discussing the program," wrote EFF Deputy Legal Director Aaron Mackey, the organization was finally able to extract some key documents about iCOP from the postal cops this month. Others were apparently destroyed.
"The disclosures include a series of bulletins created from iCOP, which show that the postal service used the program in 2020 and 2021 to monitor and circulate information about a wide range of planned protests" from "across the political spectrum," Mackey added. "They included a planned 'Million MAGA March,' a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest, and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy's home in Washington, D.C."
Reports revealed that postal investigators ran keyword searches on social media posts and created "anonymous, untraceable email and social media accounts," the better to monitor Americans' conversations. They applied Clearview AI facial recognition software to photos scraped from online platforms for comparison to a database of billions of images.
In testimony, Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale said iCOP "was developed around 2017 as part of our strategy to combat opioids and other illegal drugs in the mail" and that "the iCOP program protects the Postal Service and the public by facilitating the identification, disruption, and dismantling of individuals and organizations that use the mail or USPS online tools to facilitate black market Internet trade or other illegal activities." He claimed iCOP's mission expanded in response to threats of violence against DeJoy. Its activities were then extended to cover "situations with the potential to impact the security of our facilities and most importantly the safety of our employees." This morphed into broad surveillance and intelligence sharing with "around 70 federal, state and local agencies" through the Executive Protection Threat Intelligence Working Group.
Barksdale added that the U.S. Postal Inspection Service no longer issued law enforcement bulletins about political activities like the one published by Yahoo! News. But as EFF's Mackey emphasizes, "the documents do not say that the agency's social media surveillance stopped."
Barksdale's testimony came courtesy of congressional alarm over the Postal Service's self-appointed surveillance role. Members of Congress from both parties, including House Oversight Committee members James Comer (R–Ky.) and Carolyn Maloney (D–N.Y.), urged the Postal Service inspector general to investigate.
"These activities raise serious questions about the scope of the program, the extent of sharing of information among law enforcement agencies, and whether USPIS has the authority to conduct such an operation," they wrote.
The inspector general agreed there were grounds for concern.
"We determined that certain proactive searches iCOP conducted using an open-source intelligence tool from February to April 2021 exceeded the Postal Inspection Service's law enforcement authority," the March 2022 report confirmed. "Furthermore, we could not corroborate whether other work analysts completed from October 2018 through June 2021 was legally authorized."
The inspector general report added that postal law enforcement is supposed to have a "postal nexus" with some connection to sending and receiving mail. "However, the keywords used for iCOP in the proactive searches did not include any terms with a postal nexus. Further, the postal nexus was not documented in 122 requests and 18 reports due to a lack of requirements in the program's procedures."
The report also found that Postal Inspection Service managers didn't consult their lawyers before launching their continuously expanding surveillance program. In addition, they "did not retain information needed to ensure compliance with the Postal Inspection Service's legal authority."
In practice, EFF's Mackey notes, this resulted in the Postal Service claiming it couldn't turn over key documents because somebody dropped the hard drive they were stored on.
"Setting aside that it's unclear whether internal oversight occurred or resulted in any changes, the claim that iCOP did not infringe on First Amendment rights rings hollow," comments Mackey. "As the records disclosed show, surveilling and reporting on social media users' efforts to organize rallies and protests was a feature of iCOP."
Given the Postal Service's activities, it's probably safest to assume that all government agencies eventually get around to treating Americans as potential threats to be spied upon.

articles.title: Brickbat: The King and I
articles.content:
Thai political activist Arnon Nampa has been sentenced to two years and eight months in prison for criticizing Thailand's monarchy during a 2020 pro-democracy protest. This brings his total prison sentence to more than 34 years, all for insulting the monarch. Nampa and four other protesters were convicted under Article 112, Thailand's strict law against insulting or criticizing the king and royal family. The protest called for changes to the constitution, reforms to the monarchy, and the resignation of then-Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha. The defendants argued that their speeches were protected by the constitutional right to peaceful assembly, but the court rejected that argument. Nampa was a leading figure in the youth-driven protest movement that challenged traditional restrictions on discussing the monarchy. Since the protests began in 2020, 294 people—including 20 minors—have faced prosecution under Article 112. Critics argue that authorities have increasingly used the law to silence political opposition and restrict freedom of expression, with convictions and lengthy prison sentences discouraging public criticism of the monarchy.

articles.title: Trump Debates Mass Deportation With Himself
articles.content:
In a 60 Minutes interview that aired on Sunday night, President Donald Trump conceded that his mass deportation campaign may have contributed to the Republican rout in last week's midterm elections because "a lot of people think it's too tough." Yet on the same day he sat for the interview, Trump announced that he had picked Stephen Miller, the main architect of that policy, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Those seemingly contradictory signals reflect a conflict between Trump's "tough" instincts on immigration and his intermittent qualms about the economic and human consequences of deporting unauthorized but otherwise law-abiding residents with deep roots in their communities. Trump's ambivalence jibes with the mixed views of voters, who generally applaud efforts to police the border and expel criminals but are less comfortable with deporting peaceful and productive people who have worked and raised families in the United States for years.
Trump and his underlings have said his immigration crackdown focuses on "the worst of the worst." Yet the Cato Institute's David Bier, who looked at detainees arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in fiscal year 2026, found that 73 percent had no criminal convictions, nearly half also had no pending criminal charges, and just 5 percent had been convicted of violent offenses.
The Migration Policy Institute reported similar findings in October: During the first 18 months of Trump's second term, just one-fifth of deportees had been convicted of crimes. The organization also noted that 61 percent of deportees had lived in the United States for more than two years, while 15 percent had been here for a decade or more.
Although hardliners like Miller want to "get everybody out," Trump noted in the 60 Minutes interview, "a lot of people" think the government should deport "the rough ones," including "drug dealers," "rapists," and "killers," but "work a deal" for others, including immigrants who "in some cases" have been here for "10 and 15 years." He said a deal along those lines with the Democrats who will soon take control of Congress is "actually doable."
This is not the first time that Trump has expressed reservations about the indiscriminate approach to immigration enforcement favored by Miller. In June 2025, Trump ordered a short-lived pause on workplace raids, and the following month he said that "we're gonna work with" employers of unauthorized immigrants in the agriculture and hospitality industries.
"These people…work so hard," Trump said at a July 2025 rally in Des Moines. "They bend over all day. We don't have too many people [who] can do that."
Trump added that "some of the farmers…cry when they see [immigration raids] happen." He alluded to "cases where…people have worked for a farmer on a farm for 14, 15 years" and "then they get thrown out, pretty viciously."
Trump's conclusion: "We can't do it. We've got to work with the farmers and people that have hotels and leisure properties."
Trump revisited that theme on 60 Minutes. When "you have a woman" who is doing "a great job" as a waitress or a hotel cleaner, he said, "and all of a sudden, they're being taken out of the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing."
Last April, the Pew Research Center reported that 52 percent of Americans thought the Trump administration was doing "too much" when "it comes to deporting immigrants who are living in the U.S. illegally." In a CBS News exit poll last week, 58 percent of voters said the Trump administration's immigration enforcement had "gone too far."
They could be right, Trump admitted in the interview: "It might be too tough." While "I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," he said, "I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs" whose "one violation" was that "they came into the country illegally."
Will Trump follow through on these impulses? That depends on the outcome of his debate with Miller—and with himself.
